institution_name: Southern California Gas Company (SoCalGas) and San Diego Gas & Electric Company (SDG&E)
use_case: Runs a PLEXOS production cost model that simulates hourly least-cost dispatch of Western US generation to forecast natural gas demand from utility electric generation (UEG) customers in its California Cost Allocation Proceeding (CAP) applications (2027-2029 CAP period).
source_title: Prepared Direct Testimony of R. Fiola M. Michelle Dandridge on Behalf of SoCalGas and SDG&E (Large Electric Generation/Cogen Forecast), CAP Application A.25-09-XXX
exact_snippet_or_quote: This forecast uses the PLEXOS model (Model) developed by the software provider Energy Exemplar, Inc. The Model evaluates, in detail, the least-cost dispatch of the electricity supply to meet system demand on an hourly basis and provides results of generation unit output, including fuel burn.
why_it_supports_the_claim: First-party regulatory testimony by SoCalGas/SDG&E staff explicitly names PLEXOS (by Energy Exemplar) as the production cost model used to build their UEG natural gas demand forecast for the CAP proceeding.
notes: Evidence from search snippet of the utility's own direct testimony; PDF not downloaded. PLEXOS is used for gas-demand forecasting from electric-plant dispatch, not for electric resource planning. Same method used in the 2024-2027 CAP (testimony of Jeff Huang, socalgas.com) and prior California Gas Reports, so usage is longstanding. SDG&E is a PG&E Corp affiliate; row covers the joint filing.

use_case: ORNL researchers used PyPSA (version 0.24.0) as the power network solver, coupled with EPANET for water, to simulate network rebalancing following transmission line outages in a cascading-failure study of synthetic power and water networks for the City of Phoenix.
source_title: Cascading Failure Propagation and Perfect Storms in Interdependent Infrastructures
exact_snippet_or_quote: Using the City of Phoenix as a case study, synthetic power and water networks are constructed and coupled, and disturbances are simulated to capture cascading failure behaviors within and across power and water distribution systems. Network solvers [PyPSA (version 0.24.0) for power and EPANET (version 2.2) for water] are used to capture network rebalancing. Failures are simulated starting with transmission line outages and 120,000 simulations used to capture stochasticity in the rebalancing of power and water systems.
why_it_supports_the_claim: ORNL's own publication page states that PyPSA version 0.24.0 was used as the power network solver in their cascading-failure simulation work.
notes: First-party evidence from ORNL's publication page (snippet verbatim). Study uses a synthetic Phoenix power/water network as case study, so usage is for research simulation rather than an operational planning product. ORNL also appears in this catalogue's PLEXOS rows; this is a separate PyPSA finding.

institution_name: Stanford University (Department of Energy Resources Engineering)
use_case: Stanford Department of Energy Resources Engineering researchers (Tehranchi, Barnes, Frysztacki, Azevedo) built PyPSA-USA, an open-source framework for power system planning and capacity expansion analysis in the continental United States, built on the PyPSA framework, including transmission expansion studies under decarbonization pathways.
source_title: PyPSA-USA: A flexible open-source energy system model and optimization tool for the United States
exact_snippet_or_quote: PyPSA-USA: A flexible open-source energy system model and optimization tool for the United States by Kamran Tehranchi, Trevor Barnes, Martha Frysztacki, Ines Azevedo ... In this paper, we introduce PyPSA-USA, a novel, flexible, open-source model framework designed for power system planning in the continental United States. Built on the Python for Power System Analysis (PyPSA) framework, PyPSA-USA is highly configurable to support system operations and planning research at variable spatial and temporal scales.
why_it_supports_the_claim: The paper's author affiliations list Stanford University (and SFU/KIT), and the abstract states the tool is built on the PyPSA framework for US power system planning, directly evidencing Stanford as a first-party research user/builder.
notes: First-party authorship: PyPSA-USA is developed and maintained by the Stanford team (pypsa-usa.readthedocs.io is their documentation; the docs also reference CPUC/CAISO data for their California configuration). Stanford already has a PLEXOS row in the catalogue; this is the separate PyPSA finding. Evidence is the SSRN abstract-page snippet; full PDF not downloaded.

use_case: PJM uses PROMOD IV as its primary software for Market Efficiency analysis within the Regional Transmission Expansion Plan (RTEP), simulating hourly security-constrained commitment and dispatch for years 2025, 2029, 2032 and 2035 (with 2039 validation runs) to determine the economic benefits of transmission projects.
source_title: 2024/2025 Market Efficiency Input Assumptions - Mid-Cycle Update (TEAC informational item, January 2025)
exact_snippet_or_quote: The primary analytical software used by PJM to determine potential Market Efficiency benefits is PROMOD IV from Hitachi Energy. PROMOD IV is a production costing software application that simulates the hourly commitment and dispatch of generation to meet input load while recognizing and maintaining transmission system security limits.
why_it_supports_the_claim: This is PJM's own committee document explicitly naming PROMOD IV as the primary software for its RTEP Market Efficiency simulations.
notes: First-party PJM TEAC committee document (snippet from search result; underlying PDF not separately fetched per session rules). Corroborated by PJM's own 2017 'PJM PROMOD Overview' deck (https://www.pjm.com/-/media/DotCom/committees-groups/subcommittees/cs/20170811/20170811-item-02-pjm-promod-overview.ashx): 'PROMOD analysis is a critical component of the PJM Regional Transmission Expansion Process (RTEP)'. PJM is already in the catalogue as a PLEXOS user; this is a separate PROMOD record.

source_title: Value of Solar Study - LES Board Meeting Item 5D (citing SPP 2025 Integrated Transmission Planning Assessment Report)
source_date: SPP ITP Assessment Report dated 2025-11-25; LES board document 2026
exact_snippet_or_quote: Analyzed ... using Hitachi's PROMOD software to analyze SPP's 2025 ITP Future 1 case, representing 30% - 40% increase in current market energy prices. Source: 2025 Integrated Transmission Planning Assessment Report, Southwest Power Pool, November 25, 2025.
why_it_supports_the_claim: The LES board document attributes PROMOD use directly to SPP's own 2025 ITP Assessment Report, and Hitachi Energy's investor presentation independently names SPP as a PROMOD customer in the United States.

First-party SPP report identified by title/date in the snippet; its own URL not separately fetched. SPP is not yet in the catalogue.

use_case: MISO used PROMOD for detailed techno-economic analysis of its Long Range Transmission Planning (LRTP) Tranche 1 portfolio, modeling the Eastern Interconnection at the bus level under its Future 1 planning scenario to evaluate reliability metrics, wholesale price effects, adjusted production costs and emission reductions of new transmission projects.
source_title: Technical Appendix - PROMOD V (PROMOD) model, data, and assumptions for the Northern Missouri Grid Transformation Program (Missouri PSC)
exact_snippet_or_quote: To evaluate the LRTP Tranche 1 portfolio reliability metrics and benefits, MISO has performed detailed techno-economic analysis using PROMOD. ... PROMOD is an electric market simulation model marketed by Hitachi Energy.
why_it_supports_the_claim: The Missouri PSC technical appendix for a transmission program in MISO territory states that MISO itself performed the techno-economic analysis using PROMOD, based on MISO's own LRTP Tranche 1 data and Future 1 scenario.
notes: Third-party (regulator) attribution of MISO's own process rather than a MISO first-party document; MISO's LRTP Tranche 1 report would be the first-party source for a second look, hence candidate. MISO is already in the catalogue as a PLEXOS user; this is a separate PROMOD record.

use_case: ERCOT commissioned Aurora Energy Research to model ERCOT's resource-adequacy needs under the status-quo energy-only market design (two demand scenarios, normal and extreme weather years) and to assess the reliability and system-cost impacts of market-design changes, including variants of the Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service (DRRS) as an ancillary service and an extended Operating Reserve Demand Curve (ORDC) with a $5,000/MWh offer cap, for a November 2025 report delivered to ERCOT and reviewed at a PUCT open meeting.
source_title: Assessment of Resource Adequacy Needs in ERCOT and Impact of Market Design Changes
exact_snippet_or_quote: This report, prepared for the Electric Reliability Council of Texas, provides an assessment of resource adequacy needs in the ERCOT power market and the impact of market design changes on key reliability and system costs metrics.
why_it_supports_the_claim: A report hosted on ercot.com and explicitly 'prepared for the Electric Reliability Council of Texas' by Aurora Energy Research documents ERCOT commissioning Aurora's dispatch/capacity-expansion model to evaluate resource adequacy and market-design (DRRS/ORDC) options, which is the US use of the tool the task labels Bid3.
notes: TOOL-IDENTITY CAVEAT (reviewer must resolve): the task pairs 'Bid3' with '(Aurora Energy Research)', but my searches show BID3 is actually AFRY's (ex-Poyry) long-term planning tool deployed mainly by European TSOs (e.g. NESO/National Grid ESO, Finland, Denmark), while Aurora Energy Research's model is named 'Aurora' and is, per a Kroll M&A report, 'only deployed in the U.S. market.' This row therefore records the US use of Aurora Energy Research's 'Aurora' dispatch model under the task's 'Bid3' label. The underlying fact (ERCOT using Aurora Energy Research's model) is solid and first-party; the match to the literal string 'Bid3' is not, hence status=candidate. CORROBORATION (also first-party, ERCOT-hosted): https://www.ercot.com/files/docs/2025-12-17/20251217-Aurora-Energy-Research-Report-Workshop.pdf - 'In 2025, ERCOT engaged Aurora Energy Research to perform analysis of potential future resource adequacy conditions and the impact of different market design options, including variations of the Dispatchable Reliability Reserve Service (DRRS).' tool_explicitly_named=false because the evidence names the company 'Aurora Energy Research' (and its model 'Aurora'), not the string 'Bid3'. A separate Aurora Energy Research report for the Texas Association of Business on limiting solar/wind in ERCOT (cms-production.auroraer.com, 2025-04) shows the same tool in US use but that commissioner is a trade body, not a US ISO, so not recorded here.

use_case: Built and maintains PyPSA-Canada, a workflow-based modeling framework for power system analysis in Canada built on PyPSA, including a national model of Canada's 10 provinces divided into 23 regions, applied to analyzing Canadian power system scenarios including the Atlantic Loop.
source_title: NRCan/pypsa-canada GitHub repository (README)
exact_snippet_or_quote: pypsa_canada is a workflow-based modeling framework for power system analysis in Canada, built on top of PyPSA (Python for Power System Analysis). This tool enables comprehensive energy system optimization and planning for Canadian electricity grids.
why_it_supports_the_claim: The repository is owned by the NRCan GitHub organization and its first-party README describes a PyPSA-based framework for Canadian power system analysis.
notes: Corroborated by NRCan's own CanmetENERGY LinkedIn showcase (https://linkedin.com/showcase/canmetenergie-canmetenergy): 'During the meeting, Nathan presented PyPSA-Canada, a library and model repository tailored to the Canadian context and built on the PyPSA framework. The repository currently includes a national model representing Canada's 10 provinces, divided into 23 regions...' and by the PyPSA documentation users page: 'Natural Resources Canada (NRCan): used PyPSA create a workflow-based modeling framework for power system analysis in Canada.' Distinct from the Canada Energy Regulator (CER) already recorded (ESM-0080).

use_case: Navigant ran a 'PROMOD simulation of the Ontario electricity market' to complete a rigorous economic analysis of the Ontario Pumped Storage Project, calculating the ratepayer and CO2 emissions impacts of the project by running simulations with and without the project, and described PROMOD as an industry-standard production cost model simulating hourly chronological operation of generation and transmission resources on a nodal basis in wholesale electric markets.
source_title: Value of Pumped Storage Project Report (Ontario Pumped Storage Project)
exact_snippet_or_quote: The Navigant team completed a rigorous economic analysis using Navigant's PROMOD simulation of the Ontario electricity market, calculating the ratepayer and CO2 emissions impacts of the project by running simulations with and without the project. ... PROMOD is an industry-standard, detailed energy production cost model that simulates hourly chronological operation of generation and transmission resources on a nodal basis in wholesale electric markets.
why_it_supports_the_claim: The project report directly attributes a PROMOD-based economic analysis of the Ontario market to the Navigant team, naming both the organization and the tool for a specific Canadian use case.
notes: Verbatim quote from a search-engine snippet of the project PDF (permitted evidence standard; underlying PDF not re-fetched). Navigant is a global consultancy (later merged into Guidehouse); recorded under Canada because the modeling work was of the Ontario electricity market. Source date not stated in the snippet, so left empty. Third-party report (project website) rather than a Navigant first-person document, hence MEDIUM strength, but the quote is explicit and specific.

use_case: PSR's SDDP algorithm (paired with the OptGen capital expansion module) solves the stochastic operating module of Manitoba Hydro's mid-term planning, evaluating multistage investment and operating trade-offs under stochastic hydrothermal operation.
source_title: MEED/MH I-22a-p (U) - Mid-Term Energy and Electric Demand (MEED-22) report, Manitoba Hydro IRP regulatory review
exact_snippet_or_quote: The operating module calculates the stochastic policy that minimizes the average operating costs over the study horizon, considering uncertainties in inflows, renewable generation, equipment failures etc. This problem is solved through the Stochastic Dual Dynamic Programming algorithm (SDDP), developed by PSR. ... 'OptGen 1': uses decomposition techniques allowing the use of SDDP model to incorporate multistage trade-off evaluation considering stochastic hydrothermal operation
why_it_supports_the_claim: Manitoba Hydro's own regulatory filing describes its mid-term planning model as being solved with PSR's SDDP together with the OptGen investment module.
notes: First-party document hosted on Manitoba Hydro's own domain (hydro.mb.ca), in the IRP regulatory review folder. The document explicitly names both SDDP (operating module) and OptGen (investment module) from PSR. MEED-22 is Manitoba Hydro's 2022 Mid-Term Energy and Electric Demand report. Search-snippet evidence per session rules; original PDF not re-fetched.

use_case: SDDP applied to the medium-term optimal management of the Hydro-Québec hydroelectric system under uncertainty, accounting for water conservation, load and hydraulic constraints and stochastic inflows.
source_title: Lafond (2004): Application of the stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) method to the medium term optimal management, under uncertainty, of the Hydro-Quebec system (OSTI record 20559288)
exact_snippet_or_quote: The SDDP has been applied to the Hydro-Quebec system and has proven to be a powerful analytical tool that is well defined and based on solid concepts. It demonstrates the importance of a simplified and reliable modeling of inflow stochasticity.
why_it_supports_the_claim: The OSTI abstract of the 2004 report states explicitly that SDDP was applied to the Hydro-Québec system for medium-term optimal management.
notes: Evidence is an OSTI bibliographic abstract (third-party record of a 2004 technical report), not the report itself. Author Lafond's affiliation with Hydro-Québec is not confirmed from the snippet, and the PSR vendor spelling does not appear in the abstract (SDDP used as algorithm name). The report itself is likely Hydro-Québec's own work; a reviewer should check the full report. Search-snippet evidence per session rules; original document not re-fetched.

source_title: Using SDDP to Develop Water-Value Functions for a Multireservoir System with International Treaties, Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management, Vol 144, No 2
exact_snippet_or_quote: This paper presents the implementation of stochastic dual dynamic programming (SDDP) to generate water-value functions for operations planning of the British Columbia (BC) Hydro system.
why_it_supports_the_claim: The paper abstract states that SDDP is implemented for operations planning of the BC Hydro system to generate water-value functions under stochastic inflows and Columbia River Treaty constraints.
